messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 36
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Urban Planner
  trauma_type: Relief worker in war zone
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Old Memories: Old photos, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Shouting: Shouting
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Harm: hurt myself physically to release overwhelming feelings, Thought Suppression: I try to push them out of my mind, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Memory: Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

Vignette:
Thao is a 36-year-old urban planner who came to therapy at the urging of her partner, after months of what she described as "just not being myself." She had been a relief worker for three years in a conflict zone, coordinating shelter logistics in a region where airstrikes and ground combat were constant. The event that broke her happened on a clear afternoon. She had been driving a supply truck through a rural corridor with a local colleague when they came under small-arms fire. The truck swerved and overturned into a shallow ravine lined with tall grass and wildflowers. She remembers the smell of crushed vegetation and fuel, the sound of shouting in a language she barely understood, and the sight of her colleague’s body slumped against the dashboard. She crawled out and ran through the grass until she found a village, but she could not save him. She has not spoken of that afternoon in detail to anyone since.

In the months that followed, Thao found that old photographs—any images from that period of her life—would send her into a state she could only describe as "not being in the room." She would feel the heat of that afternoon, hear the shouting, and for a terrifying moment she would be back in the ravine. The sensation was so complete that she once dropped a coffee cup at her desk because a coworker’s sudden movement to grab a file triggered a full flashback. She had come to believe that her body was permanently on alert, that danger could arrive at any second. At night, she lay rigid in bed, her ears tuned to every creak and whisper in the apartment, unable to let her guard down enough to sleep.

She began to avoid the triggers she could name. She deleted every photo from her phone that predated her return home. She stopped going to parks or nature trails, because the sight of tall grass and open fields made her chest tighten. She flinched at shouting in the street, at arguments in the next room, at any raised voice. At work, she chose windowless meeting rooms and sat with her back to the wall. She told herself she was being practical. But the effort of staying watchful was exhausting, and the memories kept surfacing anyway. When they did, she felt a surge of rage so intense it frightened her—rage at the men who had shot at them, at the organization that had sent her there, at herself for surviving. She would dig her fingernails into her palms or, in private, press a heated hair straightener against her thigh just to feel something other than the fury. It was the only way she knew to release the pressure.

When people asked what had happened, she could not explain. The words would tangle, the timeline would collapse, and she would trail off mid-sentence, unable to finish. The memory itself felt strange to her, as though it belonged to someone else—a woman in a documentary, not the person who now sat in a clean office drawing zoning maps. She kept her mind occupied constantly. Podcasts during her commute, music at her desk, television until her eyes burned at night. If a quiet moment came, she would reach for her phone or start a new task. She had learned that stillness was dangerous.

What finally brought her to seek help was a series of mornings when she could not get out of bed. Her partner had found her staring at the ceiling, unable to speak. She knew she was losing ground. She was afraid of what the therapy would ask of her—afraid that talking about it would make the memory feel real, would make it hers. But she was also afraid of what would happen if she kept going the way she was. She wanted to stop hurting herself. She wanted to be able to look at a photograph without disappearing. She wanted to sleep. She said she did not know if she could get better, but she was willing to try.
